     ANSWER OF THE OHIO TRANSMISSION OWNERS IN OPPOSITION TO
     MOTION OF PERSISTENCE ANALYTICS GROUP LLC TO INTERVENE
             NEARLY THREE YEARS AFTER THE DEADLINE

       Pursuant to Rule 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (“Commission”),1 the Ohio Transmission Owners2 respectfully

submit this answer in opposition to the Motion of Persistence Analytics Group LLC [(“PAG”)]




       1
           18 C.F.R. § 385.213 (2026).
       2
         The Ohio Transmission Owners are American Electric Power Service Corporation, on behalf
of Ohio Power Company and AEP Ohio Transmission Company (collectively, “AEP”), FirstEnergy
Service Company, as agent for its affiliate American Transmission Systems, Inc. (“ATSI”), The Dayton
Power and Light Company d/b/a AES Ohio (“AES Ohio”), and Duke Energy Ohio, Inc. (“Duke”).
 to Intervene Out of Time,3 filed nearly three years after the deadline of November 17, 2023.4

The Motion should be denied because PAG wholly fails to demonstrate good cause under Rule

214(b)(3) and (d) to intervene so late.5

I.     BACKGROUND

       On September 28, 2023, the Ohio Office of Consumers’ Counsel (“OCC”) filed a

Complaint in the above-captioned proceeding against PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”)

and the Ohio Transmission Owners,6 alleging that the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff

(“PJM Tariff”) and Operating Agreement are unjust and unreasonable because the formula rate

protocols “lack a process for guaranteeing adequate regulatory oversight of the need, prudence,

and cost-effectiveness of Supplemental Projects in Ohio.”7 In the Complaint, OCC alleged

that regulators are failing to make the Ohio Transmission Owners prove consumer need,

prudence, and the reasonableness of the costs of Supplemental (sometimes called “local”)

transmission projects in Ohio,8 asserting that this constitutes a regulatory gap leaving Ohio

 retail consumers without any way to assure that Supplemental transmission project costs are

just and reasonable.9

       On September 29, 2023, the Commission issued a notice setting October 18, 2023 as

the comment date for this docket.10 The Commission later issued a notice extending that date

by thirty days, to November 17, 2023.11 Pursuant to Rule 210(b), that comment date also is

the date for filing a motion to intervene.12 Numerous parties moved to intervene before the

deadline, one moved to intervene out of time on November 30, 2023,13 and one moved to

intervene out of time on December 18, 2023.14 Thus, the only two motions to intervene out of

time were filed within approximately one month of the deadline. PAG’s motion, by contrast,

was filed nearly three years after the deadline.

       On November 17, 2023, the Ohio Transmission Owners answered and moved to

dismiss the Complaint and the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners protested the Complaint,

each rebutting the OCC’s assertion that any regulatory gap exists.15 In their respective

 responses to the Complaint, the Ohio Transmission Owners and the Indicated PJM

Transmission Owners explained that the Commission and Ohio regulators are correctly

operating within their proper jurisdictional authority, consistent with the open and transparent

local planning process set out in Attachment M-3 to the PJM Tariff, and that this regulatory

authority, as well as the ability of customers or their advocates to file a section 206 complaint

challenging a particular project or projects as imprudent, provides adequate oversight over

local projects.16

        On September 1, 2026, nearly three years after the deadline to intervene had passed on

October 18, 2023, PAG filed its motion to intervene and “Limited Comments.” The motion

states, inter alia, that “PAG takes no position in these comments on the ultimate disposition of

the Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel’s complaint.”17

II.     ANSWER

        PAG’s motion to intervene should be denied because it fails to demonstrate good cause

for its nearly three-year delinquency.

        Under Rule 214(b)(3), a motion to intervene filed beyond the applicable deadline—

here, as explained above, November 17, 2023—must “show good cause why the time

limitation should be waived.”18 Rule 214(d) elaborates:

        In acting on any motion to intervene filed after the period prescribed under Rule
        210, the decisional authority may consider whether:

        (i) The movant had good cause for failing to file the motion within the time
        prescribed;

Complaint and Answer Opposing Request for Fast-Track Processing of Complaint, The Office of the
Ohio Consumers’ Counsel v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al., Docket No. EL23-105-000 (filed Nov.
17, 2023) (“Protest”).
        16
             Motion to Dismiss and Answer at 5-10, 20-30; Protest at 7-15.
        17

        18
             18 C.F.R. § 385.214(b)(3).
                                                   4
          (ii) Any disruption of the proceeding might result from permitting intervention;

         (iii) The movant’s interest is not adequately represented by other parties in the
         proceeding;

         (iv) Any prejudice to, or additional burdens upon, the existing parties might
         result from permitting the intervention; and

         (v) The motion conforms to the requirements of paragraph (b) of this section.19

PAG’s motion fails to satisfy these factors and should be denied.

         At the threshold, PAG’s motion is extremely late. It was filed on September 1, 2026,

nearly three years after the applicable deadline of November 17, 2023. Even less delinquent

motions have been denied based, inter alia, on the length of the delay.20

         PAG similarly fails to make an adequate showing under the applicable factors listed

above.

         First, PAG attempts to meet the good cause showing by arguing:

         Since the complaint was filed in September 2023, however, the infrastructure-
         planning environment relevant to transmission investment has evolved
         materially. In particular, electric-system planners, regulators, utilities, large-
         load customers, investors, and public officials are confronting substantially
         greater questions regarding projected large-load growth, data-center demand,
         forecast durability, project timing, infrastructure causation, and the allocation
         of costs associated with new or accelerated transmission investment.21



         19
               18 C.F.R. § 385.214(d). The fifth factor is whether the motion complies with the
requirements of Rule 214(b). The Commission need not address that factor here because the motion
plainly fails to meet the first four factors under Rule 214(d).
         20
            See, e.g., Pembina Cochin LLC, 196 FERC ¶ 63,009, at P 4 (2026) (Presiding Administrative
Law Judge’s order denying motion to intervene that was filed “eighteen months” late). The
Commission likewise often denies motions to intervene out of time. See, e.g., Martha Coakley, Atty.
Gen. of the State of Mass., et al. v. Bangor Hydro-Electric Co., et al., 194 FERC ¶ 61,208, at P 48
(2026); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 167 FERC ¶ 61,209, at P 24 (2019) (denying later intervention
where movants merely “not aware how” a dispositive order “would impact them”), reh’g denied, 168
FERC ¶ 61,104 (2019); Power Co. of Am., L.P. v. FERC, 245 F.3d 839, 843 (D.C. Cir. 2001) (“Failure
to establish good cause [for untimely motion] is… a sufficient condition to deny intervention”).
         21
              Motion at 2.
                                                 5
 But the Complaint concerns the review process to which local transmission projects are or

should be subject, not the actual level of need for transmission investment in light of

background circumstances. This process has not changed since the filing of the Complaint

three years ago. Thus, while other aspects of the planning process may be changing as

suggested by the motion to intervene, the Attachment M-3 process that is the subject of the

Complaint has not.

        In any event, the need for transmission and other infrastructure to supply large loads is

not a new development. To the contrary, as early as late 2023 (and thus by the time that the

Organization of MISO States, the most recent intervenor before PAG, filed its motion to

intervene), reports had identified new and unprecedented forecasted load growth.22 And even

if such growth has escalated even further since 2023, that does not excuse PAG from filing its

motion in 2024 (or even 2025), as opposed to in late 2026 as it is attempting to do now.

        Second, allowing PAG to intervene so late, long after all parties have filed multiple

pleadings (the most recent of which, aside from two motions to lodge by the complainant,23

was filed on January 25, 202424), will disrupt the proceeding. PAG seeks to inject, by its own

Demand is Over (Dec. 1, 2023), excerpt available at https://www.ourenergypolicy.org/resources/the-
era-of-flat-power-demand-is-over/ (last visited Sept. 11, 2026) (“Grid planners have revised their
projections, with the nationwide electricity demand growth forecast rising from 2.6% to 4.7% over the
next five years, according to 2023 filings with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC).
This revision means that peak demand is expected to grow by 38 gigawatts (GW) through 2028,
necessitating rapid planning and construction of new generation and transmission infrastructure.”).
        23
           Complainant Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel (“OCC”) recently filed a third motion
to lodge along with a motion for expedited action, see Motion for Expedited Action and Motion to
Lodge New Information by Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel, The Office of the Ohio Consumers’
Counsel v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al., Docket No. EL23-105-000 (Aug. 27, 2026), which we
answered separately. Notably, that pleading does not concern the issues that PAG seeks to raise.
        24
           See Motion for Leave to Respond and Response of Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel
to the Transmission Owners’ Answer, The Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel v. PJM
Interconnection, L.L.C., et al., Docket No. EL23-105-000 (Jan. 25, 2024).

                                                 6
 admission, a “distinct” issue from what the parties have raised, namely “an independent

implementation and decision-assurance perspective regarding the evidence required before

infrastructure assumptions become the basis for long-lived customer or system obligations.”25

If PAG is allowed to do so, then fairness would require that the existing parties be afforded an

opportunity to respond to that distinct issue, which would complicate and disrupt the

proceeding. Such disruption is particularly unwarranted given that “PAG takes no position on

the ultimate disposition of the Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel’s complaint.”26

       Third, to the extent that PAG, a self-described “analytics firm,”27 purports to represent

the “public[] interest,”28 that interest is already adequately represented by the existing parties

to the proceeding, which include the complainant (an advocate for customers), other similar

entities from other states, transmission owners, customer organizations, and the Independent

Market Monitor for PJM.

       Fourth, for similar reasons to those addressed above under the second factor, allowing

PAG to intervene so late and to file comments on a new and distinct issue will prejudice the

parties by requiring them to prepare further submissions in response to PAG’s comments.

III.   CONCLUSION

       Wherefore, for the foregoing reasons, the Ohio Transmission Owners respectfully

request that the Commission deny PAG’s motion to intervene nearly three years after the

applicable deadline.
